The city millage is 35.05 mills, the lowest municipal rate in DeSoto County, and the city has said publicly it intends to keep that title. The typical home runs about $336,100, the highest in this file, up 1.1% year over year, with average rents near $1,940 and apartment rents up about 2%.

That price point is the whole underwriting story. At the citywide median with 20% down, even with the county's most favorable tax stack, the ratio computes to about 0.73. Olive Branch is not a cash-flow market at the median; it is a tenant-quality and appreciation market where the households renting $2,200 to $2,500 homes have logistics-manager and FedEx-pilot incomes and stay for years. The national wave of build-to-rent capital figured this out already, which is part of why entry pricing stays firm.

Files that clear here look specific: four-bedroom newer builds where rent crosses $2,300, interest-only structures that lower the qualifying payment, and 30% equity. The reassessment caveat from the rest of DeSoto County applies here too, 2025 values reset upward even as millage rates fell, so compute taxes at 15% of your actual purchase price, not the seller's history.

Inside the city limits in Forrest County, the combined levy runs about 184.3 mills, city, county, and school district together. The discipline is mechanical: pull the parcel, confirm which taxing district it actually sits in, then compute 15% of your price against that district's real millage. The Avenues clears the full city load because the entry price is low and rents near $1,400 are stout for the price point. Oak Grove clears because the stack is lighter. The citywide average clears nothing, because it blends two markets that share nothing but a mailing address. Enrollment growth may absorb it, the university plans another 5,000 to 6,000 students by 2030, but per-bedroom pricing power is no longer a one-way bet.

The lender is not being difficult; the 1007 reflects what happens if the student model breaks, which is exactly the scenario underwriting exists to price. Absorption is plausible; guaranteed it is not. The files that work here either buy product where the whole-unit rent is genuinely strong, newer four-bedrooms in Oxford Commons appraising near $2,900, or bring 30% equity so the 1007 figure covers the smaller loan. Your matched specialist structures the file on the appraiser's number from the start and lets the per-bedroom premium be your upside, not your qualification.

faqItems.question: Is the Oxford student housing supply wave a real risk?

Enrollment is growing too, 28,405 in fall 2025 with plans for 5,000 to 6,000 more by 2030. The likeliest outcome is absorption with flattening per-bedroom rents rather than a crash, which is precisely why qualifying on the whole-unit 1007 rent instead of peak student pricing is the durable structure.

faqItems.question: Does buying a duplex raise my property taxes in Mississippi?
faqItems.answer: No, and this is a genuine structural advantage over neighboring states. Mississippi assesses all non-owner-occupied real property, single-family rental or duplex alike, as Class 2 property at 15% of true value. Tennessee, by contrast, reclassifies residential property with two or more rental units as commercial at a 40% assessment, which can nearly double the tax bill on a Nashville or Memphis duplex. In Starkville the duplex pays the same 155.42-mill stack at the same 15% ratio as the house next door while producing materially more rent, which is exactly why the duplex is the signature file here.
